title: How To Praise Students And Influence Behavior https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/11/27/how-to-praise-students-and-influence-behavior/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Drawing on a personal anecdote from early in his career, Linsin argues against the common belief that bigger, louder, more frequent praise is more effective. He explains that excessive, public praise loses meaning, lowers expectations, and becomes background noise that fails to actually change behavior. His alternative is a four-part framework for meaningful praise: make it private rather than public, make it subtle through small gestures like a note or a quiet word rather than a fanfare, make it worthy by reserving it for genuinely above-expectation performance, and make it sincere, since insincere praise fails to land with students regardless of delivery. He closes with the concise formula that more praise isn't better - private, subtle, worthy, and sincere praise is what actually influences behavior.
points: Loud, frequent, public praise loses meaning over time and becomes ineffective background noise.
Private praise is more effective than public recognition in most situations.
Small, subtle gestures - a note, a smile, a quiet comment - carry more weight than showy displays.
Praise should be reserved for genuinely above-expectation performance to remain meaningful.
Praise must be sincerely felt by the teacher, or students will sense the insincerity and it will fail to motivate.
quotes: I started throwing around praise like a dog trainer with milk bones.
I’ve since discovered that this is a common belief in education; that the bigger, the more frequent, and the more over-the-top the praise is, the better.
Giving praise privately is more effective than doing it in front of the class.
Small gestures of praise are powerful. Eye contact and a smile from across the room. A note folded over and left waiting on a student’s desk. A hushed, “I knew you could do it.
Praise won’t have meaning to your students if they don’t deserve it. Only offer praise when you notice them doing something that is beyond what is a common classroom expectation.
Praise won’t have its desired effect unless you’re genuinely proud of your student(s). If you don’t feel it in your heart, they won’t feel it either.
When it comes to praising students, more isn’t better. Private, subtle, worthy, and sincere, though, are.
